stories.headline: Judge Dismisses Trump's $10 Billion Defamation Suit Against Wall Street Journal Over Epstein Birthday Letter
stories.summary:
A federal judge has thrown out President Donald Trump's $10 billion defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal, its parent company Dow Jones and Rupert Murdoch, ruling that the suit was "grasping at straws." Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed the case with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled. He had previously dismissed an earlier version of the suit that sought $20 billion in damages.

The suit stemmed from a Journal report last year on a letter bearing Trump's name that was allegedly part of a 2003 birthday book for Jeffrey Epstein, before the financier was charged with sex crimes. The paper described typewritten text framed by the hand-drawn outline of a naked woman. Trump has denied writing or signing the letter and called the story fake and defamatory.

In a 20-page ruling, Gayles found that Trump's lawyers failed to show the defendants published with "actual malice," the legal standard requiring proof that a publisher knew a statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for the truth. He cited the paper's "thoughtful and detailed investigation" and rejected the argument that Trump's denial obliged the Journal to drop the story, saying that rule would let any public figure block negative coverage simply by denying it and would run afoul of the First Amendment.

The story appeared as the administration faced bipartisan criticism over its handling of Epstein documents. Press freedom advocates are likely to welcome the ruling, while Trump allies have long argued that media outlets publish damaging stories about the president with insufficient verification. It was not immediately clear whether Trump would appeal.

stories.headline: Update: Peltola Denies Knowledge of Alleged Plot to Put Two Dan Sullivans on Alaska Ballot as DOJ Escalates Probe
stories.summary:
Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola said she knew nothing about an alleged scheme that led to two men named Dan Sullivan appearing in the Alaska Senate race. "I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent," she told voters Thursday. "I am not interested in tricking voters."

The Trump administration is escalating its inquiry. At a Friday press conference, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman said both civil and criminal investigations are ongoing, though no charges had been filed as of Friday evening. The Justice Department has reportedly begun issuing subpoenas to Democratic officials allegedly linked to the recruitment effort, according to CBS News. Later Friday, administration lawyers asked a federal judge to order state election officials, before Monday, to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher. Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward argued the step would help determine whether such rankings resulted from voter confusion.

The controversy began when The New York Times reported that people tied to Peltola's campaign and senior Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee aides tried to recruit Dan J. Sullivan as a spoiler candidate, citing text messages and interviews with 12 people. The Peltola campaign denies the reports, and Sullivan has denied any link to her campaign. The BBC said it had not independently verified the reporting.

Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and allies accuse Democrats of trying to confuse voters, and Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an official inquiry. Alaska's ranked-choice system lets voters rank both Sullivans. The race is among the tightest in the midterms, which will decide control of Congress.

stories.headline: Update: Gulf States Fear Fiercer Iranian Retaliation if US Strikes Again
stories.summary:
Gulf states fear that another US-Israeli attack on a better-prepared Iran could unleash an even more destructive war across the region, according to Bloomberg. Officials in the Gulf worry they would be left to pick up the pieces of any renewed conflict.

The concern comes as tensions remain high over Iran, with the US maintaining a naval blockade and Iran's supreme leader having ordered a "maximum" response to any renewed attack. President Trump has said Iran wants to talk, and the administration is pursuing a dual-track strategy of pressure and diplomacy.

Gulf governments, which host US forces and depend on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, would be exposed to retaliation. Their concern is that Iran has had time to prepare since earlier strikes and could respond more forcefully.

stories.headline: India's Opposition Holds Mass Delhi Rally Demanding Election Chief's Resignation Over Voter-Roll Revision
stories.summary:
Tens of thousands of people gathered at Ramlila Maidan in central Delhi on Sunday for a rally demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. The protest was organised by the opposition INDIA bloc and led by Rahul Gandhi's Congress party. It drew many of the alliance's most prominent figures, including Sonia Gandhi, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Mamata Banerjee, Akhilesh Yadav, Mehbooba Mufti, Supriya Sule and Tejashwi Yadav. Protesters chanted "Save the vote, save the country" and "Vote thief, give up power."

At the centre of the dispute is the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which has resulted in more than 130 million names being removed from India's draft voter lists. The opposition alleges that legitimate voters are being struck off and that the process could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party in future elections. The Election Commission says the exercise is meant to remove duplicate registrations and the names of people who have died, moved away or are otherwise ineligible, and that wrongly excluded voters can seek to have their names restored.

Addressing the crowd, Rahul Gandhi said the gathering represented "the voice of India's youth, women, farmers and workers" and vowed: "We will not allow democracy to be destroyed in India." Kharge said the alliance would continue its campaign until Kumar resigns. Banerjee pledged to keep fighting what she described as threats to democracy.

The BJP and the Election Commission deny the opposition's allegations. Senior BJP leader and federal minister JP Nadda called the rally a "calculated conspiracy to plunge the nation into anarchy - in the name of democracy," accusing the opposition of trying to destabilise the government. The rally is the latest in a series of protests over the roll revision, and the opposition has signalled the campaign will continue.

stories.headline: Update: More Than 320,000 Protest Across France in Third Weekend of Demonstrations as Unrest Spreads Across Europe
stories.summary:
More than 320,000 people took to the streets across France on the weekend in a third consecutive round of nationwide demonstrations against the rising cost of living and poor public services, according to the interior ministry. At least 290 protesters were arrested. Police said about 70,000 people marched in Paris, where officers fired tear gas and clashed with demonstrators.

Authorities mounted an extensive security operation to prevent a repeat of the violence, rioting and looting that took place two weeks ago. The protests come as France prepares for a general strike in the coming days, which could further disrupt transport and public services.

The unrest is not confined to France. Demonstrations were also reported in Albania, Germany and Italy, with the BBC's correspondent James Waterhouse reporting that young people are driving protests across Europe. Earlier cost-of-living protests in Germany turned violent, with shops looted.

The new developments are the latest weekend's turnout and arrest figures, the scale of the Paris march, and the spread of protests to additional European countries. Attention now turns to the planned general strike and whether the government can contain the unrest.

stories.headline: Update: Analysis Links Serbia's Student Landslide to Hungary's Ousting of Orbán
stories.summary:
Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić and Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who met in northern Serbia last November, are both now out of power. Orbán was defeated in April by Péter Magyar's Tisza party. Last Sunday, a student movement less than two years old won Serbia's parliamentary elections by a landslide.

The two movements differ in structure: Tisza is built around its leader, while Serbia's Student List says it has no leadership. Both were driven by young, tech-savvy voters, with turnout of 79% in Hungary and 69% in Serbia. Activists used AI tools to analyze data, identify threats to the vote and mobilize tens of thousands of election monitors.

A Hungarian civic group, DE, sent 70 monitors to Serbia and ran workshops over the summer sharing its methods. A key technique was identifying polling districts in advance where unusually high governing-party results suggested intimidation or chain voting. Student activist Péter Klemm of Subotica said masked groups of Vučić supporters gathered near polling stations from about 16:00, prompting mobile teams to film events, with 20 to 30 volunteers at threatened sites acting as a deterrent.

Orbán and Vučić had held power for 16 and 14 years respectively, taking over state institutions and building overlapping business interests. They shared ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, and backed Bosnian Serb separatist leader Milorad Dodik. The new element is this comparative analysis of how the two governments fell and what it means for the region.

stories.headline: How US Mail-In Ballots Are Secured and Counted Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
Ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3, BBC Verify visited an election center in Maryland to examine how mail-in ballots are processed and counted. The report details security measures including CCTV monitoring and zip ties used to secure ballots.

President Donald Trump continues to make unsubstantiated claims that mail-in voting leads to widespread fraud. The BBC notes that every US state allows some form of postal voting, a method the president says he has used himself in the past.

Voting rules and regulations vary by state, and the report offers a behind-the-scenes look at one jurisdiction's procedures. The piece comes as the midterms approach, with disputes over election administration, including subpoenas and monitoring, already prominent in the campaign. Supporters of stricter voting rules argue they protect election integrity, while election officials and many Democrats say existing safeguards are robust.

stories.headline: Ethiopian PM Puts Cabinet Ministers Through Military Training Amid Security Tensions
stories.summary:
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put cabinet ministers and other senior officials through military training, saying armed forces discipline can build stronger leaders and advance national development. Photos he shared on social media show him taking part in exercises with ministers, deputy ministers and heads of institutions at the Hurso military training center.

Participants include House of Federation Speaker Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba. The move is unusual, as senior civilian officials in Ethiopia are rarely seen undergoing such training. It is unclear when the training began or how long it will last.

Abiy said leadership must be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable, adding: "Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory." The training comes amid fighting in parts of Tigray, conflict in Amhara, insecurity in Oromia, and heightened tensions with Eritrea, raising concerns about renewed war between the two countries.
